description.value: The study used event-related fMRI in 26 healthy participants to compare the neural correlates of conditional and syllogistic deductive reasoning, separately examining premise encoding and premise integration.

design.value: We used event-related fMRI, in the same group of subjects, to compare reasoning-related activity associated with conditional and syllogistic deductive problems. We separately assessed the encoding and integration stages of both propositional (conditional) and quantified (syllogistic) arguments.

description.value: Average accuracy for conditional and main-set syllogistic problems.
Reaction times on integrable and non-integrable sentences for both conditional and syllogistic problems; only correctly answered trials were used to compute RTs.
Proportion of responses that were wrong but consistent with the atmosphere heuristic in the nonheuristic set of syllogistic problems.

name.value: response times at the encoding stage

source_definition.value: The activation estimates were corrected for the response times at the encoding stage.

name.value: interaction “problem type (syllogisms vs. conditionals) × task (reasoning vs. memory)”

source_definition.value: The interaction “problem type (syllogisms vs. conditionals) × task (reasoning vs. memory)” confirmed that the reasoning-related activation during encoding was greater for syllogisms than for conditional premises.

name.value: interaction problem type (syllogisms vs. conditionals) × condition (integrable vs. non-integrable)

source_definition.value: We assessed the presence of areas showing a difference between the integration effect for syllogisms and the integration effect for conditionals: i.e. with the interaction problem type (syllogisms vs. conditionals) × condition (integrable vs. non-integrable).

description.value: Twenty-six healthy subjects (aged 25 years on average, SD: 5.0; 15 males) participated in the experiment. All were right-handed, had normal vision, with no neurological or psychiatric history.

task_description.value: Participants performed conditional and categorical syllogistic deductive reasoning and memory trials during event-related fMRI. Reasoning trials presented two or three premises serially; participants read each premise, integrated premises when possible to draw a conclusion, and selected the valid or inferred conclusion from four alternatives. Memory trials presented a single premise followed by four alternatives for literal recognition.

instructions.value: Subjects were informed they would do either a “reasoning” or a “memory” task, depending on the letter presented at the beginning of each trial (“R” for a reasoning and “M” for a memory trial). In reasoning trials, participants were asked to read each premise and whenever possible, to draw a new conclusion promptly and accurately. In memory trials, subjects were told to read and remember sentences carefully for fast recognition from among four subsequently presented sentences.

stimuli.value: All sentences described the qualities of an unspecified “thing” by means of nonexistent two-syllabic adjectives with a plausible phonological structure in Italian. The 132 deductive problems comprised 72 categorical syllogisms and 60 conditional problems; 40 memory trials were also administered.

task_performance_measures.value: Average accuracy for conditional and main-set syllogistic problems.
Reaction times on integrable and non-integrable sentences for both conditional and syllogistic problems.
Heuristic index: proportion of responses that were wrong but consistent with the atmosphere heuristic in the nonheuristic set of syllogistic problems.

instrument.value: 3T Siemens Allegra head scanner (Siemens, Erlangen, Germany)

description.value: Blood oxygenation level-dependent (BOLD) contrast was obtained using echo planar T2*-weighted imaging (EPI). Acquisition of 32 transverse slices provided coverage of the whole cerebral cortex. Repetition time was 2.08 s, echo time was 30 ms, in-plane resolution was 3 mm × 3 mm, and slice thickness and gap were 2.5 mm and 1.25 mm, respectively. The experimental phase was divided into four fMRI runs with 43 trials for each run. On average 1561 volumes per subject were available for analysis, ranging from 1355 to 1748 volumes.

description.value: The absence of gross structural brain abnormalities was checked on structural scans.

The first four image volumes of each run were discarded to allow for stabilization of longitudinal magnetization. Preprocessing included rigid-body transformation (realignment) and slice timing to correct for head movement and slice acquisition delays. Images were normalized to MNI space using nonlinear warping implemented in SPM2, using the mean of all functional volumes as a template, and then smoothed with an 8 mm full-width at half maximum Gaussian filter. The time series for each participant was high-pass filtered at 128 s and prewhitened by means of an autoregressive model AR(1).

steps.value: The first four image volumes of each run were discarded.
Rigid-body transformation (realignment) to correct for head movement.
Slice timing to correct for slice acquisition delays.
Normalization to MNI space using nonlinear warping implemented in SPM2 and the mean of all functional volumes as a template.
Smoothing with a Gaussian filter of 8 mm full-width at half maximum.
Prewhitening by means of an autoregressive model AR(1).

model_settings.value: A 2 × 2 ANOVA on RTs on P1 used the factors task (reasoning vs. memory) and type of problem (syllogistic vs. conditional problems). A second 2 × 2 ANOVA on RTs from P2 used integrability (integrable vs. nonintegrable premises) and type of problem (syllogistic vs. conditional problems).

The data were best fitted at every voxel for each participant using a combination of effects of interest. The effects of interest were the times of onset of 18 event types within each of the four fMRI runs. Events were modeled as miniblocks of duration corresponding to timing stimuli shown on screen. Eight theoretically interesting event types corresponded to two 2 × 2 factorial designs: P1 task type (reasoning vs. memory) × problem type (conditionals vs. syllogisms), and P2 integrability (integrable vs. nonintegrable sentences) × problem type (conditionals vs. syllogisms). Error trials were modeled separately from correct trials.

The four contrast images per subject underwent a second step comprising two ANOVAs, one for encoding and one for integration, that modeled the mean of each effect. Linear compounds compared these effects using between-subject rather than between-scan variance. Correction for nonsphericity accounted for possible differences in error variance across conditions and nonindependent error terms for repeated measures analysis. P-values corrected for multiple comparisons were assigned using Family Wise Error at the voxel level, considering the whole brain as the volume of interest. For the interaction, P-values corrected for multiple comparisons were computed at cluster level with P < 0.01 uncorrected at voxel level.

Six regions of interest were identified on the basis of the activation map of syllogisms during integration. The average integration effect for syllogistic problems across all voxels in each ROI was extracted for every subject. PCA was run on the resulting 26 × 6 matrix; after orthogonal rotation, the varimax procedure was used.

Memory trials required participants to read and remember a sentence for fast recognition from four subsequently presented sentences.
Propositional reasoning problems using logical connectives such as “if…then”; the study used three logical forms for integrable conditional problems.
Quantified predicative statements forming categorical syllogisms; 72 categorical syllogisms were administered, including integrable main-set and nonheuristic problems.

The first stage of deduction, in which premises are stored in working memory.
The second stage of deduction, in which premises are linked together to generate a conclusion whenever possible.
